source_read: PDF, pp. 377–382 (all 6 pages read; Tables 1–2 and Figures 1–4 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi)

claims.overstatement: None for the parts this source carries. The claim is more cautious than the source, whose abstract concludes that methamphetamine 'leads to' the reduction. Minor: in this study abstinence ran from 2 weeks to 36 months (3 of 15 participants 11–36 months), so 'days to months' slightly understates the upper end.
claims.note: Numbers from this source checked against Table 2: caudate Bmax/Kd 1.3 vs 1.8 gives 27.8% and putamen 1.5 vs 1.9 gives 21.05% (printed 21.1%); 15 users vs 18 controls. My standardized differences from the table means and SDs: about 1.9 (caudate) and 2.0 (putamen), approximate because values are printed to one decimal. The 6 vs 10 study, the pooled g and its interval do not come from this source. 'Differences that predate use' is not discussed by the authors; it follows from the cross-sectional design (no pre-use scan).

anchors.extracted: DAT availability (Bmax/Kd), users (n=15) vs controls (n=18): caudate 1.3 (SD 0.2) vs 1.8 (SD 0.3); putamen 1.5 (SD 0.2) vs 1.9 (SD 0.2); two-tailed t>4.7, df=31, p<0.0001; text gives 27.8% (caudate) and 21.1% (putamen) lower. Distribution volume also lower in caudate (22.8 vs 29.8) and putamen (24.9 vs 31.7) but not cerebellum; K1 (tracer delivery) did not differ.

Users: DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence, entry criterion of at least 0.5 g/day, 5 days/week, for 2 years; mean use 11 years (SD 6); urine-confirmed abstinence of at least 2 weeks; time since last use mean 5.9 months (SD 9.0, range 0.5–36); 12 had last used 2–24 weeks before, 3 had abstained 11–36 months. Recruited from rehabilitation centres; 18 controls by advertisement. Users 6 men/9 women, age 32, estimated IQ 100; controls 12 men/6 women, age 31, IQ 107.

Individual Bmax/Kd values plotted by group: several users lie inside the control range in both caudate and putamen (lowest control values about 1.3 caudate and 1.6 putamen; highest user values about 1.8 and 2.0).

DAT not correlated with days since last use (r<0.11, df=14, p>0.70) or with self-reported dose (r<0.37, p>0.17); caudate DAT correlated with years of use (r=0.54, p<0.05; putamen r=0.47, p<0.08), sign not printed. The three participants abstinent 11–36 months lie below the control means (caudate about 1.35–1.43, putamen about 1.48–1.6) but their caudate values are within the control range.

anchors.locator: Discussion, last two paragraphs (left column into right column)
anchors.extracted: Authors state the reduction could reflect lower transporter expression or degeneration of terminals, that it is unknown which, and cite a post-mortem study with DAT but not VMAT2 reductions interpreted as terminal persistence; further studies needed.

key_findings.correction: Optional precision: the three long-abstinent users are below the control means, but their caudate values (about 1.35–1.43) lie within the control range (lowest control about 1.3) (Figure 3 vs Figure 2, p. 379).

Data correct. The correlations are in the Results' 2nd (last) paragraph, starting 'Because the estimates...' (p. 379, right column, continuing on p. 380); Results has only two paragraphs. Figure 4 is on p. 380.
The same point is also made in the preceding paragraph (p. 381, left column: reduction could reflect lower transporter expression or terminal degeneration).

reporting_issues.note: Table 1 average daily dose range 0.3–10.0 g vs entry criterion of at least 0.5 g/day (p. 378). I did not check the 0.25 g/day criterion in Volkow 2001b here; see my volkow_2001b file.
Figure 4 (p. 380) shows negative slopes for the two timed motor tasks and positive slopes for the recall scores, all printed as positive r.
df=14 used throughout for n=15 correlations (pp. 379–380), while the t-tests correctly use df=31.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high agreed. For the DAT outcome itself, selection of the reported result is less of a concern than for the cognitive outcomes; the high rating is driven by the cognitive reporting.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. In addition, the discussion speculates on a later Parkinson's risk from the combination of methamphetamine-related and age-related DAT decline (p. 380), which the data do not test.

missed: The authors note that the reduction was of similar size in caudate and putamen, unlike Parkinson's disease, where the putamen is more affected, and infer a different mechanism (p. 380, Discussion, right column). This bears on the encyclopedia's claim that the pattern differs from Parkinson's disease (cl_meth_dopamine_damage), which this source could support but does not currently anchor.

Figure 4 (p. 380): one participant with the lowest DAT (Bmax/Kd about 1.0) sits at the extreme of all four panels; with n=15 and no robustness check reported, the within-user correlations may depend heavily on that participant.
The authors also state that three users had DAT within the range reported for mild Parkinson's disease without showing those values or extrapyramidal assessments (p. 380).
